use.en: Use it for habits, routines, facts and things that are always true.
use.bn: অভ্যাস, প্রতিদিনের কাজ, সত্য ঘটনা আর চিরসত্য বোঝাতে।

examples: She walks to school every day.
The sun rises in the east.
recap.tip: With he, she or it, add -s to the verb: he runs, she watches.

questions.prompt: My brother ___ football every Sunday.

options.why: “My brother” is he, so the verb needs -s: plays.
“Is playing” is for right now, but “every Sunday” is a habit.
“Played” is the past, but “every Sunday” is about what he usually does.

questions.explanation: “Every Sunday” is a habit, and the subject is he (my brother), so the verb takes -s.

questions.prompt: Water ___ at 100 °C.

options.why: Water is “it”, so the verb needs -s: boils.
“Is boiling” means it is happening right now, not that it is always true.
A fact that is always true stays in the present, not the past.

questions.explanation: This is a scientific fact, always true, so we use the simple present.

questions.prompt: ___ your parents speak English?

options.why: “Does” goes with he, she or it, not with “your parents” (they).
“Are” would need speaking: Are your parents speaking? Here the verb is plain “speak”.
“Is” goes with one person or thing, and it does not go with plain “speak”.

questions.explanation: “Your parents” is they, so the question starts with Do.

questions.prompt: Riya ___ like spicy food.

options.why: “Don’t” goes with I, you, we and they. Riya is she, so use doesn’t.
“Isn’t” does not go with an action verb like “like”.
English needs a helper here: Riya doesn’t like…, not “Riya not like”.

questions.explanation: Riya is she, so the negative is doesn’t + the plain verb (like).

questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?

options.text: The sun rise in the east.
options.why: “The sun” is it, so the verb needs -s: rises.

options.text: The sun rises in the east.
The sun is rise in the east.
options.why: Don’t mix “is” with the plain verb. Say “rises”.

options.text: The sun rising in the east.
options.why: This has no proper verb. A sentence needs “rises” (or “is rising”).

questions.explanation: A fact that is always true, with he / she / it, so the verb takes -s: rises.

use.en: Use it for actions happening right now, or for a short time around now.
use.bn: এখন যে কাজ চলছে, বা কিছু সময়ের জন্য চলছে, তা বোঝাতে।

form.pattern: Not: am / is / are + not + verb-ing
Question: Am / Is / Are + subject + verb-ing?

examples: Look! The cat is climbing the tree.
We are learning tenses this week.
recap.tip: Some verbs about the mind or feelings, like know, like and want, are rarely used with -ing.

questions.prompt: Look! The baby ___.

options.why: “Sleeps” is for habits. “Look!” tells us it is happening now.
“The baby” is it, and “Look!” needs the -ing form: is sleeping.
“Slept” is the past, but “Look!” means right now.

questions.explanation: “Look!” shows it is happening right now: is + sleeping.

questions.prompt: We ___ for the bus right now.

options.why: “Waits” is for he / she / it habits, not “we” right now.
“Is” goes with he, she or it. With “we”, use “are”.
“Wait” is for habits. “Right now” needs “are waiting”.

questions.explanation: “Right now” + we → are + waiting.

questions.prompt: Shh! I ___ my homework.

options.why: “I do my homework” is a habit. “Shh!” means it is happening now.
“Does” never goes with I.
After am, the verb needs -ing: am doing.

questions.explanation: “Shh!” shows it is happening now; with I we use am + doing.

questions.prompt: Why ___ you laughing?

options.why: “Do” goes with the plain verb: Why do you laugh? Here we have “laughing”.
“Is” goes with he, she or it, not with you.
“Does” goes with he, she or it, and with the plain verb.

questions.explanation: The verb is “laughing”, so we need are with you.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?

options.text: The children are swimming in the pond.

options.why: “Know” is a thinking verb that is rarely used with -ing. Say “She knows the answer.”
“They” goes with are, not is.
“He” goes with is, not are.

questions.explanation: Children are they → are + swimming. Correct!

use.en: Use it for something that happened before now when the time is not said, for life experiences, and for things that started in the past and are still true.
use.bn: কাজটি শেষ হয়েছে কিন্তু তার ফল এখনো আছে, বা জীবনের অভিজ্ঞতা বোঝাতে (কখন হয়েছে বলা থাকে না)।

form.pattern: Not: have / has + not + past participle
Question: Have / Has + subject + past participle?

examples: I have just finished my lunch.
She has visited Sylhet twice.
recap.tip: Don’t use it with a finished time like yesterday or last week. Use the simple past there.

questions.prompt: She has already ___ her lunch.

options.why: “Ate” is the simple past. After has, use the past participle: eaten.
After has, the verb must be the past participle: eaten.
“Has eating” is not English. Use “has eaten”.

questions.explanation: After has, we use the past participle: eaten.

questions.prompt: ___ you ever ___ an elephant?

options.why: “Did” is for a finished time in the past. “Ever” about your whole life uses Have … seen.
After have, use the past participle (seen), not the past (saw).
“Has” goes with he, she or it. With you, use Have.

questions.explanation: “Ever” asks about life experience: Have you ever seen…?

questions.prompt: We have lived in Dhaka ___ 2019.

options.why: “For” goes with a length of time, like “for five years”. 2019 is a starting point, so use since.
With the present perfect, use “since 2019”, not “from 2019”.
“Ago” goes with the simple past: “We moved to Dhaka five years ago.”

questions.explanation: Since + a starting point in time (2019).

questions.prompt: Tom ___ his homework yet.

options.why: After did / didn’t, use the plain verb, and “yet” fits better with hasn’t finished.
Tom is he, so use hasn’t, not haven’t.
“Isn’t finish” is not English. Use “hasn’t finished”.

questions.explanation: “Yet” in a negative sentence → has not (hasn’t) + finished.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?

options.text: I have seen that film yesterday.
options.why: “Yesterday” is a finished time, so use the simple past: I saw that film yesterday.
The past participle of write is written: She has written a letter.
“He” goes with has, not have.

questions.explanation: “Just” + have + past participle (arrived) is correct.

use.en: Use it for an action that started in the past and is still going on now, especially to say how long.
use.bn: অতীতে শুরু হয়ে এখনো চলছে এমন কাজ, কতক্ষণ ধরে চলছে তা বোঝাতে।

form.pattern: Not: have / has + not + been + verb-ing
Question: Have / Has + subject + been + verb-ing?

examples: It has been raining since morning.
I have been reading this book for a week.
recap.tip: It answers “How long?”: for two hours, since Monday, all day.

questions.prompt: It ___ since morning.

options.why: “Is raining” says it is raining now, but not how long. With “since”, use has been raining.
“Rains” is for habits and facts, not for something going on since morning.
“It” goes with has, not have.

questions.explanation: It started in the morning and is still going on: has been + raining.

questions.prompt: I’m still waiting! I ___ here for two hours.

options.why: “For two hours” needs the present perfect continuous: have been standing.
“Stood” is finished, but “I’m still waiting” tells us it is still going on.
“I” goes with have, not has.

questions.explanation: Started two hours ago and still going on: have been + standing.

questions.prompt: Your eyes are red. ___ you been crying?

options.why: “Are you been” is not English. Use “Have you been crying?”
“Has” goes with he, she or it. With you, use Have.
“Did” goes with the plain verb (Did you cry?), not with been.

questions.explanation: The question form is Have + you + been + verb-ing.

questions.prompt: She has been learning the piano ___ three years.

options.why: “Since” goes with a starting point, like “since 2021”. Three years is a length of time.
“Ago” goes with the simple past: She started three years ago.
We say “for three years” with this tense, not “from three years”.

questions.explanation: For + a length of time (three years).

questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?

options.text: They have been played chess all afternoon.
options.why: After been, use the -ing form: have been playing.

options.text: We has been talking for an hour.
options.why: “We” goes with have, not has.

options.text: He has been working in the garden all day.
I have been know her for years.
options.why: “Know” is not used with -ing here. Say “I have known her for years.”

questions.explanation: has + been + working: the action has gone on all day.

use.en: Use it for actions that started and finished at a known time in the past.
use.bn: অতীতের নির্দিষ্ট সময়ে যে কাজ হয়ে শেষ হয়েছে, তা বোঝাতে।

examples: We visited Grandma yesterday.
I lost my pencil last week.
recap.tip: After did and didn’t, the verb goes back to its plain form: Did you go? (not “Did you went?”)

questions.prompt: We ___ to Cox’s Bazar last summer.

options.why: “Go” is the present. “Last summer” needs the past: went.
Don’t use the present perfect with a finished time like “last summer”.
“Goes” is present, and it goes with he, she or it.

questions.explanation: “Last summer” is a finished time, so we use the past form of go: went.

questions.prompt: She didn’t ___ the bus this morning.

options.why: After didn’t, the verb goes back to its plain form: didn’t miss.
After didn’t, use the plain verb, without -es.
After didn’t, use the plain verb, not the -ing form.

questions.explanation: After didn’t, use the plain verb: miss.

questions.prompt: ___ you call your grandmother yesterday?

options.why: “Do” is for the present, but “yesterday” is in the past.
“Have” doesn’t go with a finished time like “yesterday”, and it would need “called”.
“Were you call” is not English. Use “Did you call?”

questions.explanation: Past questions use Did + the plain verb (call).

questions.prompt: Two days ago, Arif ___ his arm.

options.why: “Breaks” is the present. “Ago” needs the past: broke.
Don’t use the present perfect with “ago”.
“Broken” is the past participle. On its own it needs has or had.

questions.explanation: “Two days ago” is a finished time. The past of break is broke.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?

options.why: “Seen” needs have or had. The simple past is “saw”: I saw him last night.
“Buy” is irregular. Its past is bought: She bought a new dress.
After didn’t, use the plain verb: He didn’t go to school.

questions.explanation: A finished action at a known past time: watched.

use.en: Use it for an action that was in progress at a moment in the past, often when something else happened.
use.bn: অতীতের কোনো এক সময়ে যে কাজ চলছিল, তা বোঝাতে (প্রায়ই তখন অন্য কিছু ঘটেছিল)।

examples: I was reading when the lights went out.
While we were playing, it started to rain.
recap.tip: The long action uses was / were + -ing; the short action that interrupts it uses the simple past.

questions.prompt: At 8 pm yesterday, I ___ dinner.

options.why: “Ate” shows a finished action. “At 8 pm” asks what was going on at that moment.
“Am eating” is now, but “yesterday” is in the past.
“I” goes with was, not were.

questions.explanation: At that moment the action was in progress: was + eating.

questions.prompt: They ___ football when it started to rain.

options.why: “They” goes with were, not was.
“Played” would mean they began playing when the rain started. The game was already going on.
“Are playing” is now, but the story is in the past.

questions.explanation: The game was in progress when the rain started: were + playing.

questions.prompt: While Mum was cooking, Dad ___ the table.

options.why: “Sets” is the present, but the sentence is in the past.
“Is setting” is now. Match the past: was setting.
The present perfect does not fit a past story with “while … was cooking”.

questions.explanation: Two actions in progress at the same time: was cooking … was setting.

questions.prompt: What ___ you doing when I phoned?

options.why: “You” always goes with were, not was.
“Did” goes with the plain verb (What did you do?), not with “doing”.
“Are” is now, but “when I phoned” is in the past.

questions.explanation: With you and “doing”, we use were.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?

options.text: I was read a book when the lights went out.
options.why: After was, use the -ing form: I was reading a book.

options.text: The dog was barking all night.

options.why: “She” goes with was, not were.
“We” goes with were, not was.

questions.explanation: The dog is it → was + barking.

use.en: Use it for an action that was finished before another action or time in the past.
use.bn: অতীতের দুটি কাজের মধ্যে যেটি আগে শেষ হয়েছিল, তা বোঝাতে।

examples: When we arrived, the film had started.
She had never flown before that trip.
recap.tip: Think of two past events: the earlier one takes had + past participle.

questions.prompt: When we reached the station, the train ___.

options.why: “Left” would mean it left at the moment we arrived. To show it left earlier, use had left.
“Has left” is the present perfect. The story is in the past, so use had left.
“Was leave” is not English. Use “had left”.

questions.explanation: The train left first, before we reached the station: had + left.

questions.prompt: She ___ never ___ snow before she visited Nepal.

options.why: The visit is in the past, so the earlier time needs had, not has.
After had, use the past participle (seen), not the past (saw).
“Did never see” is not English. Use “had never seen”.

questions.explanation: Not seeing snow came before the visit: had + seen.

questions.prompt: By the time the teacher arrived, we ___ the test.

options.why: The story is in the past (“arrived”), so use had, not have.
“Finish” is the present. We need had finished.
After had, use the past participle: finished.

questions.explanation: The test ended before the teacher arrived: had + finished.

questions.prompt: I couldn’t buy the book because I ___ my money.

options.why: The sentence is in the past (“couldn’t”), so use had lost.
After had, use the past participle: lost.
“Am losing” is now, but this story is in the past.

questions.explanation: Losing the money came before not buying the book: had + lost.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?

options.text: After he had eaten breakfast, he went to school.
After he had ate breakfast, he went to school.
options.why: After had, use the past participle: eaten, not ate.

options.text: After he has eaten breakfast, he went to school.
options.why: “Went” is past, so the earlier action needs had, not has.

options.text: After he had eating breakfast, he went to school.
options.why: After had, use the past participle (eaten), not the -ing form.

questions.explanation: First he ate (had eaten), then he went: correct!

use.en: Use it for an action that had been going on for some time before another moment in the past.
use.bn: অতীতের কোনো সময়ের আগে থেকে কিছুক্ষণ ধরে যে কাজ চলছিল, তা বোঝাতে।

examples: We had been walking for an hour when it got dark.
His shoes were wet because he had been playing in the rain.
recap.tip: It is like the present perfect continuous, moved back into the past: has been → had been.

questions.prompt: We ___ for an hour when the bus finally came.

options.why: “Came” is past, so use had been, not have been.
“Were waited” is not English. Use “had been waiting”.
“Are waiting” is now, but the story is in the past.

questions.explanation: The waiting went on for an hour before the bus came: had been + waiting.

questions.prompt: His clothes were muddy because he ___ in the rain.

options.why: “Were muddy” is past, so use had been playing.
After been, use the -ing form: playing.
“Is playing” is now, but the sentence is about the past.

questions.explanation: The playing went on before we saw the muddy clothes: had been + playing.

questions.prompt: How long ___ she been living there before she moved?

options.why: “Moved” is past, so use had, not has.
“Was been” is not English. Use “had been”.
“Did” goes with the plain verb, not with “been living”.

questions.explanation: Before a past event (moved): had + been + living.

questions.prompt: They had been ___ for two hours before they took a break.

options.why: After had been, the verb needs -ing: walking.
After had been, use -ing (walking), not -ed.
After had been, use -ing, not -s.

questions.explanation: After had been, use the -ing form: walking.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?

options.text: I had been study all night.
options.why: After been, use the -ing form: I had been studying all night.

options.text: They has been talking for hours before the bell rang.
options.why: Before a past event, use had been: They had been talking.
Use “been”, not “being”: He had been running.

options.text: She had been working at the bank for ten years when she retired.

questions.explanation: had + been + working, for ten years before she retired: correct!

use.en: Use will for predictions, promises, offers and decisions made right now. Use be going to for plans, or when you can see something is about to happen.
use.bn: ভবিষ্যতে যা ঘটবে, প্রতিশ্রুতি বা এখনই নেওয়া সিদ্ধান্ত বোঝাতে (will); পরিকল্পনা বোঝাতে (going to)।

form.pattern: am / is / are + going to + verb

examples: I will call you tomorrow.
Look at the clouds. It is going to rain.
recap.tip: After will, the verb never changes: he will go (not “he will goes”).

questions.prompt: I’m sure you ___ the exam.

options.why: “I’m sure” is about the future result, so use will pass.
“Passed” is the past, but the exam is still to come.
After will, use the plain verb: will pass.

questions.explanation: A prediction about the future: will + pass.

questions.prompt: It’s hot in here. I ___ open the window.

options.why: “I am open” is not English. A decision made now uses will.
“Did” is the past, but you are about to open it.
“Was” is the past and does not go with “open” here.

questions.explanation: A decision made right now: I will (I’ll) open the window.

questions.prompt: Look at those dark clouds! It ___ rain.

options.why: It needs is: It is going to rain.
After will, there is no “to”: will rain.
The form is “is going to”, with -ing.

questions.explanation: You can see it is about to happen, so we use is going to.

questions.prompt: ___ you help me with this box, please?

options.why: “Do you help” asks about a habit, not a request for now.
“Are you help” is not English.
“Did” is the past, but the help is needed now or soon.

questions.explanation: Asking someone to do something: Will you help me…?

questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?

options.why: After will, the verb stays plain: She will come.
There is no “to” after will: We will visit Grandma.
“Will” never takes -s: He will call you.

questions.explanation: will + not + the plain verb (be): correct!

use.en: Use it for an action that will be in progress at a certain time in the future.
use.bn: ভবিষ্যতের কোনো নির্দিষ্ট সময়ে যে কাজ চলতে থাকবে, তা বোঝাতে।

examples: At this time tomorrow, I will be flying to Chattogram.
Don’t call at nine. We will be having dinner.
recap.tip: Picture the future moment: what will be happening then?

questions.prompt: At this time tomorrow, I ___ on a plane.

options.why: “Will fly” is a simple prediction. “At this time tomorrow” asks what will be going on: will be flying.
“At this time tomorrow” is the future; use will be flying.
After will be, use the -ing form: flying.

questions.explanation: At that future moment the flight will be in progress: will be + flying.

questions.prompt: Don’t call at 9. We ___ dinner then.

options.why: That means dinner will already be over at 9, so a call wouldn’t disturb you.
“Have” is the present, not a future moment.
“Had” is the past, but 9 o’clock is still to come.

questions.explanation: At 9 the dinner will be in progress: will be + having.

questions.prompt: This time next week, they ___ on the beach.

options.why: “This time next week” describes what will be going on, so use will be lying.
After will be, use the -ing form: lying.
“Are lie” is not English.

questions.explanation: In progress at a future moment: will be + lying.

questions.prompt: ___ you be using the computer tonight? I need it.

options.why: “Are you be” is not English. Use “Will you be using?”
“Do you be” is not English.
“Have you be” is not English. Use “Will you be using?”

questions.explanation: The question form is Will + you + be + verb-ing.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?

options.text: She will singing at the concert on Friday evening.
options.why: You need be: will be singing.

options.text: She will be sing at the concert on Friday evening.
options.why: After be, use the -ing form: singing.

options.text: She will be singing at the concert on Friday evening.
She be will singing at the concert on Friday evening.
options.why: The order is will + be + verb-ing.

questions.explanation: will + be + singing: correct!

use.en: Use it for an action that will be finished before a certain time in the future.
use.bn: ভবিষ্যতের কোনো সময়ের আগেই যে কাজ শেষ হয়ে যাবে, তা বোঝাতে।

form.pattern: Not: will not have + past participle
Question: Will + subject + have + past participle?

examples: By 6 o’clock, I will have finished my homework.
By the time you arrive, we will have left.
recap.tip: Look for “by”: by Monday, by the time… The action is done before then.

questions.prompt: By 6 o’clock, she ___ all her homework.

options.why: After will, you need have + past participle: will have finished.
“By 6 o’clock” is in the future, so use will have finished.
After have, use the past participle: finished.

questions.explanation: Done before 6 o’clock: will + have + finished.

questions.prompt: By the time you wake up, we ___ for the airport.

options.why: “Will leaving” is not English. Use “will have left”.
“Had left” is about the past, but “you wake up” is in the future.
After have, use the past participle: left.

questions.explanation: We leave before you wake up: will + have + left.

questions.prompt: They ___ the bridge by 2027.

options.why: The order is will + have + past participle.
After have, use the past participle: built.
“By 2027” is in the future, so it needs will: will have built.

questions.explanation: Finished before 2027: will + have + built.

questions.prompt: ___ you have finished the book by Monday?

options.why: “Have you have” is not English. Use “Will you have finished?”
“Did” is the past, but Monday is still to come.
“Are you have” is not English.

questions.explanation: The question form is Will + you + have + past participle.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?

options.text: By next year, she will has learned to swim.
options.why: After will, use have (never has).

options.text: By next year, she will have learned to swim.
By next year, she will have learn to swim.
options.why: After have, use the past participle: learned.

options.text: By next year, she will learned have to swim.
options.why: The order is will + have + past participle.

questions.explanation: will + have + learned, done before next year: correct!

use.en: Use it to say how long an action will have been going on by a certain time in the future.
use.bn: ভবিষ্যতের কোনো সময় পর্যন্ত কোনো কাজ কতক্ষণ ধরে চলতে থাকবে, তা বোঝাতে।

form.pattern: Not: will not have been + verb-ing
form.example: She won’t have been waiting long.

form.pattern: Question: Will + subject + have been + verb-ing?
form.example: Will you have been living here for a year?

examples: By December, I will have been working here for five years.
By 10 pm, the children will have been watching TV for four hours.
recap.tip: It answers “How long, by then?”. You will usually see both “for” and “by”.

questions.prompt: By December, I ___ here for five years.

options.why: After will be, use the -ing form, and “for five years by December” needs will have been working.
You need been: will have been working.
“By December” is in the future, so it needs will: will have been working.

questions.explanation: By December the work will have gone on for five years: will have been + working.

questions.prompt: When she finishes the race, she ___ for three hours.

options.why: The order is will + have + been + verb-ing.
You need have: will have been running.
The race finishes in the future, so use will have been running.

questions.explanation: How long, up to a future moment: will have been + running.

questions.prompt: By 10 pm, the children ___ TV for four hours!

options.why: The order is will + have + been + verb-ing.
“Will be watched” is passive and means someone watches the children.
“Are watching” is now. “By 10 pm … for four hours” needs will have been watching.

questions.explanation: By 10 pm, four hours of watching: will have been + watching.

questions.prompt: By next month, we will have been ___ English for a year.

options.why: After been, the verb needs -ing: learning.
After been, use -ing (learning) in this tense.
After been, use -ing, not -s.

questions.explanation: After will have been, use the -ing form: learning.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?

options.text: By noon, he will have been driving for six hours.
By noon, he will has been driving for six hours.
options.why: After will, use have (never has).

options.text: By noon, he will have be driving for six hours.
options.why: Use “been”, not “be”: will have been driving.

options.text: By noon, he will have been drive for six hours.
options.why: After been, use the -ing form: driving.

questions.explanation: will + have + been + driving: correct!
